description: We are hoping to bridge young minds and the unexplored and undiscovered resources of space by creating a opportunity for fresh and innovative minds to see and learn of space and NASA
summary:
Mars: Last Line of Defence is a mobile-friendly, interactive mission trainer that lets young learners command a crewed Mars mission and experience the trade-offs behind real spaceflight. Players explore a 3D Mars with 51 proposed landing sites, choose a landing zone, then take command of the crew and manage life support, power, oxygen and hull integrity while crises unfold, such as a solar storm, a failing oxygen tank or a rover running low on power.

Each decision is explained afterwards, so students learn why NASA crews make the calls they do. This addresses the challenge by turning engineering trade-offs into tangible, fun choices instead of oversimplified facts.

The game is connected to real NASA data (DONKI solar storms and CMEs, OSDR, RadLab radiation doses, plus APOD and near-Earth object feeds) through a secure Netlify proxy, with an offline archive fallback. Players learn that radiation shielding, power and food production determine whether a mission fails or succeeds. Built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, it needs no install and runs in any browser.
details:
Mars: Last Line of Defence is a browser-based interactive mission trainer for young learners. Players explore a 3D Mars with 51 proposed human landing sites, choose a site, then take command of a crew and keep life support, power, oxygen and hull integrity running through emergencies such as solar storms, a failed oxygen tank or a rover short on power. After every decision the game explains what real NASA crews do and why, so students feel the engineering trade-offs instead of memorising facts.

Benefits: it makes radiation shielding, power budgeting and risk decisions tangible and fun, and it runs on any phone or computer with no install.

Impact: it helps students understand why Mars missions succeed or fail and builds interest in space science and engineering.

Tools: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, three.js for the 3D globe, Netlify for hosting, and a Netlify serverless function that proxies NASA APIs so the key is not exposed. Live NASA data (DONKI solar storms, OSDR, RadLab, APOD, NEO, planetary K-index) is shown in the DATA tab, with an offline archive fallback.

Creativity: real mission scenarios and live space-weather data are combined into one playable story.
projectRefs: NASA Exploration Zone Workshop 2015 (landing site proposals)
